briefing.text: The hypothesis requires a community/area-level income exposure (e.g. census-tract or zip-code median household income, Area Deprivation Index, Yost index). Before any modelling, search every column name and every '#' description line in all clinical files (and other files) for income, SES, deprivation, poverty, zip, tract, census or ancestry terms, and record exactly which exposure and covariate variables exist. If the exposure is genuinely absent, the question cannot be answered by testing some other variable instead.
briefing.reason: Whether the exposure variable exists decides which labels are even possible; a header skim may miss it, so the teams need to check all files explicitly first.

briefing.text: Do not substitute proxies (race, smoking, PSA, disease extent, vital status, etc.) for community income. Race and socioeconomic status are distinct constructs; an association between race (or any other proxy) and 8q gain is not evidence about income adjusted for race. Confirm that the exposure you analyse is literally an area-level income measure.
briefing.reason: Proxy substitution is the most likely way to produce a spurious True/False on this hypothesis.

briefing.text: The hypothesis adjusts for both race AND genetic ancestry. Self-reported race is not genetic ancestry (admixture varies widely within race groups). Look for an ancestry column (e.g. % African/European ancestry, ancestry cluster). If present, include it as a covariate alongside race; if absent, state explicitly that the ancestry adjustment the hypothesis specifies cannot be performed.
briefing.reason: The hypothesis has a specific adjustment set; teams must check whether it can be met rather than silently adjusting for race only.

briefing.text: data_clinical_sample.txt already contains an 8Q_ARM call (Gain/Neutral/...). Use it as the primary 8q outcome. Re-deriving 8q status from data_cna_hg19.seg with an ad-hoc log2 threshold gives different calls because purity and ploidy shrink the observed log2 ratio (a pure single-copy gain is only ~0.58) and panel probes on the arm are sparse; use seg-derived calls only as a sensitivity check and report their agreement with 8Q_ARM.
briefing.reason: Determines how the outcome variable is defined; ad-hoc thresholds could change results.

briefing.text: 8q gain frequency rises strongly with disease progression (primary < metastasis; hormone-sensitive < castration-resistant). If any income association is tested, cross-tabulate 8Q_ARM against SAMPLE_TYPE, TISSUE_TYPE, DISEASE_EXTENT, M_STAGE and Gleason, and adjust for or stratify by them where imbalanced. Also use one sample per patient for patient-level analysis.
briefing.reason: Stage/sample type is a strong confounder of any socioeconomic-8q association.

briefing.text: Non-White race groups are typically small in single-centre prostate cohorts, so adjusting for several sparse race categories can cause sparse-data bias or separation in logistic regression. Tabulate 8q gain by race and covariate levels; if cells are empty or near-empty, collapse rare categories, use Firth penalised logistic regression, and report confidence intervals, not just p-values.
briefing.reason: Affects the validity of any race-adjusted model the teams fit.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assumed that a missing exposure (community income) makes the hypothesis untestable, so the label must be 'Not verifiable' rather than 'False'; neither team argued the label boundary explicitly against the task's definitions.
Both assumed that self-reported RACE cannot serve as, or be combined with anything to form, a genetic-ancestry covariate, and that no per-patient ancestry signal sits in the genomic files.
Both assumed that column headers and description lines reveal every variable; neither reported checking the cell values of all clinical columns for a coded area-level SES field.
unused_evidence: data_mutations.txt has population allele-frequency columns (AFR_MAF, EUR_MAF, EAS_MAF, ExAC_AF_* etc.). These are database frequencies per variant, not per-patient ancestry; neither team said so. They cannot supply income, so they do not change the label.

Patient columns SMOKING, PSA, M_STAGE, DISEASE_EXTENT, VITAL_STATUS and sample columns SAMPLE_TYPE, TISSUE_TYPE and 8Q_ARM='Not called' (120) were not used. None encodes income, so ignoring them cannot change a label that rests on the exposure being absent.
The RACE column holds only White/Black/Asian (2069 patients), with no Other/Unknown values. This may mean the cohort was already filtered by race. Neither team said whether this matters.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A said its keyword search covered only headers and the first part of large files. It reasoned the gap away and did not close it with a full-file search of cell values.
Team B named inferring ancestry from germline data as its weak point. It noted correctly that this would not supply income, so the point does not bear on the label.
second_readings: The hypothesis could be read as 'is 8q gain associated with race/ancestry', with income as the main claim. The exposure named in the hypothesis is community-level income, though. Any reading that drops income tests a different claim, so a second reading does not rescue testability.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed 'Not verifiable' highly. I checked the patient and sample columns myself: there is no community-income variable of any kind, only 8Q_ARM and self-reported RACE. The hypothesis's exposure is therefore absent, and no proxy is legitimate. The remaining doubts are about how thorough the searches were, not about the label.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your weakest point says the search scanned only headers and the first part of large files. Run a full-file, case-insensitive search of every cell value in all seven files (not only headers) for income, SES, deprivation, zip, census or area-level terms, and list the distinct values of every clinical column. Does any coded area-level SES variable appear, and does that change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Under the task's definitions, 'False' needs the relevant variables to be identifiable and 'Not verifiable' needs them to be absent. Write down which of the hypothesis's variables (exposure, outcome, covariates) you found in the data. Does the absence of the exposure alone fix the label, or would anything in the data let you identify it?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your audit covered column headers and descriptions. Tabulate the distinct values of every clinical column and search the cell values of all files, including the population-frequency columns in the mutation table, for any per-patient income or ancestry information. Does anything turn up that changes your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: RACE takes only three values with no Other/Unknown. Check whether the patient table looks pre-filtered by race, and whether every patient has a sample with an 8Q_ARM call (note the 120 'Not called'). Does either finding bear on whether the hypothesis is testable, or is the label fixed by the missing income variable regardless?
